title: Deterministic approximation scheme for graph cover times
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the expected cover time of simple random walk from a specified starting vertex of an arbitrary finite connected undirected simple graph? Specifically, does there exist one deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every integer \(q\ge2\), there are constants \(C_q,a_q>0\) for which every allowed \(n\)-vertex input \((G,v,q)\) is processed within \(C_q(n+1)^{a_q}\) bit operations and the output rational number \(\widehat C\ge0\) satisfies
\[\left|\widehat C-C(G,v)\right|\le\frac{C(G,v)}q?\]
Here \(C(G,v)\) is defined below. The runtime is polynomial in graph size for every fixed accuracy \(1/q\); its exponent may depend on \(q\). This restores the relative-approximation question actually stated by Aldous and Fill, rather than the unsupported exact-output wording in the imported draft.
why: Cover time is a global measure of how efficiently a random walk explores a network. It is readily estimated by randomized simulation, while deterministic evaluation must account for the distribution of entire exploration histories. A scheme for arbitrary graphs would resolve a concrete derandomization question about an important graph parameter, with accuracy beyond universal constant-factor estimates.
status_note: On 2026-09-14, the original Aldous–Fill HTML subsection was read directly after the older separate PDF proved text-extraction-incompatible. It specifies arbitrary fixed relative accuracy. The 2017 notes, published Ding–Lee–Peres paper, Feige–Zeitouni manuscript and Meka’s 2015 full text were compared against the restored target. A bounded later-work search found no all-graph supplied-start deterministic PTAS; source-open status records that limited check.

importance.reason: A persistent deterministic-versus-randomized approximation question for a fundamental global exploration statistic. Arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on all graphs asks for more than the known universal constant-factor comparison or special-family algorithms.
importance.basis: Individual recovery of Aldous–Fill’s original error convention, comparison with the 2017 textbook summary, and checks of the tree, constant-factor and Gaussian-process results.

sentences: The cover time is the expected number of random-walk steps needed to visit every vertex.
This card asks for a deterministic approximation scheme from any specified starting vertex of an arbitrary connected graph.
For each fixed relative accuracy, the runtime must be polynomial in graph size.
The original source asks for approximation, so the imported demand for exact output has been corrected.
Known constant-factor and restricted-family results do not provide the full all-graph guarantee stated here.

definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. It is promised connected. Its encoding consists of \(n\) in unary followed by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix, a binary starting label \(v\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the integer accuracy parameter \(q\ge2\) in binary, with standard self-delimiting integer fields. All graph families and degrees are allowed; in particular there is no bounded-degree or rapid-mixing promise.

For \(n\ge2\), let \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the discrete-time walk with \(X_0=v\). At each step it independently chooses a uniformly random neighbor of its current vertex. It has no added holding probability. Define
\[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=V(G)\},\qquad C(G,v)=\mathbb E_v[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}].\]
The initial vertex is already visited at time zero, and time counts edge traversals. There is no requirement to return to \(v\) after the last new vertex is visited. For \(n=1\), put \(C(G,v)=0\). Connectedness guarantees finite expectation. The quantity \(\max_v C(G,v)\), often called the graph’s cover time, is related but is not substituted for the supplied-start expectation.

The algorithm is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no random bits, advice or sampling oracle. Input processing, rational arithmetic and output writing count toward the runtime. Its output is a pair of binary integers representing a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. The required inequality holds for every input, not merely with high probability. When \(n=1\), it requires output zero.

The integer \(q\) represents reciprocal relative accuracy. This discretization covers any fixed requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). The constants \(C_q,a_q\) are independent of the graph and the starting vertex. No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is demanded; that would be the stronger fully polynomial scheme. Nor is an exact numerator and denominator for the unknown expectation demanded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that an algorithm with the displayed correctness and runtime guarantees exists, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must work at arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on every allowed graph and starting vertex. A constant-factor estimate, a randomized approximation, a theorem restricted to trees or a promise on hitting times, and a procedure that computes only the worst-start maximum do not establish the stated scheme. An exponential-time exact formula by itself does not establish the polynomial-time guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Section 6.8.3 explicitly introduces numerical evaluation of the supplied-start expectation up to a fixed factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\), then asks for deterministic polynomial time. The older imported title “exact cover time” omitted this convention. This review restores the original accuracy and starting-vertex scope; exact computation remains a stronger possible route to a positive answer, not a requirement.

The 2017 textbook notes describe exponential-size exact computation and then cite Aldous–Fill’s question in compressed form. They also record the later constant-factor approximation. Reading the original accuracy convention avoids treating those sentences as a new explicitly exact-output conjecture.

Ding, Lee and Peres give a deterministic constant-factor approximation for the maximum expected cover time over starting vertices. Their theorem resolves that weaker approximation question; neither the precision nor the starting-vertex guarantee is the full target of this card.

Feige and Zeitouni obtain a fully polynomial approximation for trees. Their main theorem concerns cover and return, and Section 3.2 extends the method to ordinary cover time from a specified vertex. The tree restriction is essential to the scope of the cited result.

Meka’s 2015 Gaussian-process approximation theorem has a cover-time application on bounded-degree graph sequences satisfying \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}=o(t_{\mathrm{cov}})\), as specified in Section 1.1. Here \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}\) is the maximum expected time to hit one vertex from another and \(t_{\mathrm{cov}}=\max_v C(G,v)\). The application is qualified by that assumption and does not assert this card’s all-graph, supplied-start guarantee.
